maths_ocr_h.1.3.summary: Mastering the ordering of fractions, decimals, and percentages requires translating them into a single, uniform format—typically decimals or common denominators—before comparing their values. Examiners at Grade 9 expect fluent conversions, precise use of strict and non-strict inequality symbols, and the ability to handle negative rational numbers in exam-style contexts. These revision notes provide a rigorous framework to secure full marks across non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: To compare numbers across different mathematical representations, you must convert all values into a single common format. Decimals are generally the easiest format for direct comparison, though converting everything to percentages or fractions with a common denominator is equally valid.
bullets: Convert all mixed numbers to improper fractions or decimals first.
Convert all percentages to decimals by dividing by 100.
Convert all fractions to decimals by performing short or long division.
Ensure all numbers are presented to the same number of decimal places or significant figures for a fair visual comparison.

callouts.p: Always convert to decimals when using a calculator paper, or to fractions with a common denominator when forced onto a non-calculator paper.
When asked to order numbers given in a mixed list, always write your final answer using the original numbers provided in the question, not your intermediate conversion steps.

fig.cap: Converting mixed representations into a uniform decimal format for direct comparison on a number line.

core.p: Inequalities form the rigorous mathematical language used to state the relative size and ordering of numbers. You must know the strict definitions and directional properties of each symbol.
bullets: "<" means strictly less than (does not include equality).
">" means strictly greater than.
"<=" means less than or equal to.
">=" means greater than or equal to.

head: Symbol
Name
Example Statement
Meaning
rows: a is to the left of b
a is to the right of b
a is less than or equal to b
a is greater than or equal to b

callouts.p: A mathematical statement comparing two values, showing that one is strictly greater than, greater than or equal to, less than, or less than or equal to another value.
The open side of the inequality symbol always faces the larger number: e.g., 0.8 > 3/4.

core.p: Converting fractions to decimals is achieved by dividing the numerator by the denominator using bus-stop division or by scaling the denominator to a power of 10.
bullets: Division method: Numerator divided by denominator (e.g., 3 / 8 = 0.375).
Equivalent fraction method: Scale denominator to 10, 100, or 1000 (e.g., 3 / 25 = 12 / 100 = 0.12).
Recognize common terminating fractions instantly: halves, quarters, fifths, eighths, tenths.
Be prepared for recurring decimals resulting from division by 3, 6, 7, 9, or 11.

callouts.p: 1/8 = 0.125, 3/8 = 0.375, 5/8 = 0.625, 7/8 = 0.875. Knowing these saves crucial time in exams.

core.p: Percentages are simply fractions out of 100. Converting them into decimals or fractions allows seamless integration into ordered sequences.
bullets: Percentage to decimal: Divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places to the left).
Percentage to fraction: Write over 100 and simplify fully (e.g., 35% = 35 / 100 = 7 / 20).
Handle percentages greater than 100% (e.g., 125% = 1.25 = 5 / 4).
Handle fractional percentages (e.g., 3.5% = 0.035 = 7 / 200).

callouts.p: Do not confuse 4% with 0.4. 4% means 4 out of 100, which is 0.04.

core.h: Ordering Negative Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages
core.p: Negative numbers reverse our intuitive sense of magnitude: the larger the absolute digits of a negative number, the smaller its actual value on the number line.
bullets: -0.5 is greater than -0.8 because -0.5 is closer to zero.
Always plot negative values on a mental number line to verify correct ascending or descending order.
Zero sits strictly between negative and positive rational numbers.

callouts.p: Think of negative numbers as debt. Having a debt of £10 (-10) is worse than having a debt of £5 (-5), so -10 < -5.

fig.cap: Number line demonstrating negative rational number ordering where values decrease as they move left.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" rx="10" fill="#fef2f2" stroke="#fecaca" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="360" y2="120" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><line x1="100" y1="110" x2="100" y2="130" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="100" y="95" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">-0.8</text><line x1="180" y1="110" x2="180" y2="130" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="95" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">-3/4</text><line x1="260" y1="110" x2="260" y2="130" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="260" y="95" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">-0.5</text><text x="200" y="170" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#7f1d1d" font-weight="bold">Ascending order: -0.8, -3/4, -0.5</text></svg>

core.p: Higher tier OCR papers frequently include recurring decimals represented by dot notation (e.g., 0.3...) in ordering questions. You must expand these decimals to multiple decimal places to compare them accurately.
bullets: Expand dot notation: 0.3... means 0.333333...
Expand mixed recurring decimals: 0.23... means 0.233333...
Compare digit by digit from left to right.

callouts.p: Line up at least 4 decimal places for each recurring decimal before comparing digits.

core.p: Exam questions explicitly state the required direction of sorting. Misinterpreting ascending for descending is a common source of lost marks despite correct preliminary calculations.
bullets: Ascending order: Smallest to largest (increasing values, left to right on a number line).
Descending order: Largest to smallest (decreasing values, right to left on a number line).
Double-check your final sequence against the question wording before moving on.
Ensure all separators (commas or inequality signs) are used correctly.

callouts.p: Read the command word twice. 'Ascending' = Climb up. 'Descending' = Descend down.

core.p: At Grade 9, OCR papers combine fractions, decimals, and percentages with powers, roots, or surds within the same ordering question.
bullets: Evaluate square roots and cube roots first (e.g., sqrt(0.25) = 0.5).
Evaluate index laws and negative powers (e.g., 2^(-2) = 1/4 = 0.25).
Convert all evaluated terms into standard decimals before ordering.
Check domain restrictions for negative bases raised to fractional powers.

callouts.p: Write the decimal equivalent underneath each complex term before attempting to sequence them.

core.p: Higher tier exams require chaining multiple numbers together using inequality symbols to demonstrate strict ordering across a range.
bullets: Write chained inequalities cleanly: a < b < c.
Ensure all inequality signs face the correct direction throughout the chain.
Verify that every adjacent pair satisfies the inequality condition.
Do not mix strict (<) and non-strict (<=) symbols unless specified by interval notation.

callouts.p: A sequence of inequalities comparing three or more numbers simultaneously, such as 0.2 < 1/4 < 3/10.

core.p: When a non-calculator paper prevents decimal conversion by long division, finding a lowest common denominator (LCD) is essential.
bullets: Find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of all denominators.
Scale each numerator by the same factor used on its denominator.
Compare the resulting numerators directly.
Example: Compare 3/4 and 4/5 -> LCD is 20 -> 15/20 and 16/20 -> 15/20 < 16/20.

callouts.p: To compare two fractions a/b and c/d quickly, cross-multiply: compare ad and bc. If ad < bc, then a/b < c/d.

analogy.p: Imagine runners crossing a finish line where times are recorded in different formats: seconds as decimals (9.8s), fractions of a minute (1/6 min), and percentage improvements (102% of baseline). To rank the runners from first place (fastest/smallest time) to last place, you must convert all their records into the exact same unit (seconds). The analogy breaks down because in a race, smaller numbers are better (faster times), whereas in standard ordering of quantities, larger numbers are greater.

terms.d: Arranging numbers from smallest value to largest value.
Arranging numbers from largest value to smallest value.
A mathematical relation comparing two values or expressions, indicating that one is strictly greater, greater than or equal to, strictly less, or less than or equal to another.
Any number that can be expressed as the quotient or fraction p/q of two integers, where the denominator q is not equal to zero.
A decimal representation of a number whose digits repeat infinitely in periodic patterns after the decimal point.
A decimal that has a finite number of digits after the decimal point.
A common multiple of the denominators of two or more fractions, enabling direct comparison of their numerators.
A number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100, denoted by the symbol %.
An inequality relation using strictly less than (<) or strictly greater than (>) symbols.
An inequality relation allowing equality, using less than or equal to (<=) or greater than or equal to (>=) symbols.
Fractions that represent the same proportion or numerical value despite having different numerators and denominators.
A straight line with numbers placed at corresponding intervals along its length, used for visual comparison of magnitude.

mistakes.w: Ordering numbers based on their original integer appearance without converting units (e.g., placing 85% after 0.9 because 85 is larger than 9).
mistakes.r: Convert all values to a common format (e.g., decimals 0.85 and 0.9) before comparing magnitude.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to write the final answer using the original numbers given in the question.
mistakes.r: Always map your ordered decimal/fraction list back to the exact format presented in the exam paper.

mistakes.w: Believing that -0.8 is greater than -0.5 because 8 is greater than 5.
mistakes.r: Remember that negative numbers decrease in value as their absolute magnitude increases; -0.5 is closer to zero and thus greater than -0.8.

mistakes.w: Writing descending order when ascending was requested.
mistakes.r: Carefully underline the words 'ascending' or 'descending' in the exam question before writing your answer.

mistakes.w: Treating 0.3... as 0.3 when comparing recurring decimals.
mistakes.r: Expand recurring decimals to at least 3 or 4 decimal places (0.3333) to see the true relative size.

mistakes.w: Failing to include inequality symbols when a question explicitly asks to insert '<' or '>' between values.
mistakes.r: Ensure the requested inequality symbols are clearly written between each pair of compared numbers.

exam.q: Write the following numbers in order of size, starting with the smallest: 0.65, 2/3, 63%, 0.605.
exam.tip: Convert fractions and percentages to decimals with three decimal places.

exam.q: Insert the correct inequality sign (< or >) between: 5/8 [ ] 62%
model: Convert 5/8 to a decimal or percentage: 5/8 = 0.625 or 62.5%.
exam.tip: Convert both numbers to percentages for quick comparison.

exam.q: Write the following in ascending order: -0.4, -2/5, -0.45, -44%.
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with negative decimal ordering.

exam.q: Which is larger: 3/7 or 0.428? You must show your working.
model: Convert 3/7 to a decimal: 3 divide by 7 = 0.42857...
exam.tip: Perform division to at least 4 decimal places on non-calculator papers.

exam.q: Write the following numbers in descending order: 0.72, 7/10, 71.5%, 0.725...
exam.tip: Descending means largest first.

exam.q: Fill in the missing inequality symbol: sqrt(0.16) [ ] 2/5
model: State equality or use correct non-strict inequality: sqrt(0.16) = 2/5 (or equivalent).
exam.tip: Remember square roots of decimals can result in larger numbers than the original radicand.

exam.q: Order from smallest to largest: 1.4, sqrt(2), 145%, 13/9.
exam.tip: Use your calculator efficiently to find decimal equivalents for surds.

exam.q: Write a chained inequality for the following numbers in ascending order: 0.55, 4/7, 56%.
exam.tip: Check that every adjacent pair satisfies the inequality direction.

exam.q: Which of the following is the smallest? A) 5/9, B) 0.55, C) 54%, D) sqrt(0.3)
model: Convert all options to decimals: A = 0.555..., B = 0.550, C = 0.540, D = 0.5477...
exam.tip: Evaluate multiple-choice options methodically by converting every single one.

exam.q: Explain why 0.31 recurring is greater than 0.31.
model: Compare digit in the third decimal place: 3 > 0, hence 0.31... > 0.31.
exam.tip: Mention place value explicitly to gain full marks for mathematical reasoning.

worked.q: Order the following numbers in ascending order, showing all working: 3/5, 58%, 0.61, sqrt(0.36).
steps: Order from smallest to largest using original numbers: 58%, 3/5 (or sqrt(0.36)), sqrt(0.36) (or 3/5), 0.61.
worked.ans: 58%, 3/5, sqrt(0.36), 0.61 (Note: 3/5 and sqrt(0.36) are both equal to 0.60, so either order for those two is accepted).

worked.q: Insert inequality symbols to complete the correct statement: -0.75 [ ] -4/5 [ ] -70%.
steps: Recall negative number ordering rules: larger absolute digits mean smaller values.

maths_ocr_h.1.2.summary: Mastering percentages under OCR J560 Higher tier requires seamless fluency across conversions, calculating parts of quantities, exact percentage change computations, and applying simple interest formulas. These foundational operations form the bedrock of financial mathematics and proportional reasoning in Papers 4, 5, and 6. Achieving a grade 9 depends on rigorous control over multiplier notation, reverse percentage setups, and recognizing linear growth patterns.

core.p: Percentages represent parts per hundred, serving as a universal language for comparisons. Converting accurately between percentages, decimals, and fractions is an absolute prerequisite for advanced multiplicative reasoning.
bullets: To convert a percentage to a fraction, write the number over 100 and simplify fully.
To convert a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places left).
To convert a fraction to a percentage, multiply by 100% or scale the denominator to 100.

callouts.p: A proportion or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100, denoted by the symbol %.
Do not confuse 4% with 0.4. 4% means 4 parts out of 100, which is 0.04.

fig.cap: Visualizing conversions between fractions, decimals, and percentages using a triple-axis flow model.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="30" y="90" width="90" height="60" rx="6" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="75" y="125" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Fraction</text><rect x="155" y="90" width="90" height="60" rx="6" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="125" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Decimal</text><rect x="280" y="90" width="90" height="60" rx="6" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="325" y="125" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Percentage</text><path d="M 120 110 Q 137 90 155 110" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><path d="M 155 130 Q 137 150 120 130" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><text x="137" y="85" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb" text-anchor="middle">÷ denom</text><path d="M 245 110 Q 262 90 280 110" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 280 130 Q 262 150 245 130" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2"/><text x="262" y="85" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a" text-anchor="middle">× 100</text></svg>

core.p: Non-calculator arithmetic relies on breaking percentages down into manageable, additive building blocks such as 10%, 5%, 1%, and 50%.
bullets: To find 10%, divide the quantity by 10.
To find 1%, divide the quantity by 100.
To find 5%, find 10% and halve it.
Build complex percentages by combining blocks (e.g., 35% = 30% + 5% or 35% = 3 x 10% + 5%).

callouts.p: Always state your intermediate steps clearly in non-calc papers so examiners can award method marks.
To check 15% of 80, find 10% (8) plus 5% (4) to get 12.

core.p: Calculator papers demand efficiency. Using **decimal multipliers** is faster, less prone to rounding errors, and prepares you for exponential growth topics later.
bullets: A multiplier is the decimal equivalent of the percentage.
To find 45% of 320, calculate 0.45 x 320.
To find 125% of 84, calculate 1.25 x 84.
Never round intermediate decimal answers during multi-step calculator calculations.

callouts.p: A single decimal number by which a quantity is multiplied to effect a percentage increase, decrease, or part-calculation.
Avoid relying on the % button on your calculator; writing out the decimal multiplier prevents structural confusion in multi-step problems.

core.p: Adapting quantities by adding or removing a percentage requires understanding how multipliers scale a base value relative to 100%.
bullets: For a percentage increase, add the percentage to 100% and convert to a decimal multiplier (e.g., 12% increase becomes multiplier 1.12).
For a percentage decrease, subtract the percentage from 100% and convert to a decimal multiplier (e.g., 18% decrease becomes multiplier 0.82).
Formula: New Value = Original Value x Multiplier.
A multiplier less than 1 decreases the quantity; a multiplier greater than 1 increases it.

callouts.p: Finding 85% of an amount directly gives a 15% decrease in one calculation, rather than finding 15% and subtracting.

core.p: Comparing an old value to a new value requires a standard formula based on the **original** amount as the reference denominator.
bullets: Formula: Percentage Change = ((New Value - Original Value) / Original Value) x 100.
If the result is positive, it is a percentage increase.
If the result is negative, it is a percentage decrease.
The denominator is ALWAYS the original starting value, never the new value.

callouts.p: The extent to which a variable gains or loses value, expressed as a percentage of its original amount.
Using the new value as the denominator is the most common zero-mark error in percentage change questions.

fig.cap: Structure of the percentage change formula, highlighting the critical original value denominator.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="20" width="360" height="200" rx="8" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="55" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Percentage Change Formula</text><rect x="70" y="80" width="260" height="45" rx="6" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="108" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">New Value - Original Value</text><line x1="70" y1="140" x2="330" y2="140" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="110" y="155" width="180" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="180" font-size="13" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Original Value</text><text x="345" y="162" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#16a34a">× 100</text></svg>

core.p: When a problem gives you the final value after a percentage change and asks for the original amount, you must use **inverse operations** (division, not multiplication).
bullets: Identify the multiplier used for the forward process.
Set up the equation: Original Value x Multiplier = Final Value.
Rearrange to solve: Original Value = Final Value / Multiplier.
Never find the percentage of the final value and subtract it; this is a circular error.

callouts.p: After a 20% increase to 300, the original is 300 / 1.25? No! 300 / 1.20 = 250.
If a price increased, your original value MUST be smaller than the final value.

core.p: Simple interest calculates earnings or debt based solely on the **original principal amount** for every time period, creating linear growth.
bullets: Formula: I = P x R x T / 100, where P is Principal, R is annual rate percentage, and T is time in years.
The interest added each year is constant because it is never calculated on accumulated interest.
Total Amount = Principal + Total Interest.
Useful for baseline financial comparisons, though rarely reflecting real-world bank compounding.

callouts.p: Interest calculated on the initial principal only, yielding a fixed monetary amount per time interval.

core.p: Grade 9 questions combine percentage changes, simple interest, and proportional reasoning into complex multi-stage real-world contexts.
bullets: Break multi-stage problems into chronological steps.
Label each intermediate value clearly to maintain examiner trail marks.
Watch for phrasing like 'increased by 10% and then decreased by 10%'; remember multipliers do not cancel out (1.1 x 0.9 = 0.99, a 1% net decrease).
Check units and currency formatting in final answers.

callouts.p: A 10% increase followed by a 10% increase is NOT a 20% increase; use successive multipliers: 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21 (21% increase).

core.p: Higher tier OCR papers frequently integrate percentages into algebraic expressions, requiring you to express changes in terms of unknown variables.
bullets: Represent an unknown quantity as x.
An increase of p% on x is written as (1 + p/100)x.
Formulate equations combining percentage statements with perimeter, area, or financial totals.
Factorise expressions to solve for unknown percentage rates.

callouts.p: Treat percentage multipliers as standard algebraic coefficients when solving equations.

core.p: Comparing datasets of different sizes requires converting raw scores into standard percentage terms to ensure valid mathematical evaluation.
bullets: Convert each score into a percentage: (Score / Total) x 100.
State percentages to a consistent degree of accuracy (usually 1 decimal place or significant figures).
Provide a concluding statement explicitly answering the comparative question posed.
Beware of absolute numbers versus proportional percentages.

callouts.p: Always write a concluding sentence matching your calculated percentages to the context of the question.

core.p: When numbers are rounded before percentage calculations are applied, bounds propagate through the multiplier, creating upper and lower limits for the final result.
bullets: Find the lower and upper bounds of the original quantity using standard rounding rules (UDLB).
Apply the percentage multiplier to both bounds independently.
State the resulting range clearly.
Pay strict attention to inequality notation when required.

callouts.p: Never round intermediate bound calculations; keep full calculator precision until the final stated line.

core.p: Depreciation represents a percentage decrease over time, mirroring simple or compound models applied to depreciating assets like vehicles or machinery.
bullets: Linear (straight-line) depreciation is calculated identically to simple interest, subtracting a fixed monetary amount per year.
Percentage depreciation uses a multiplier less than 1.
Understand the distinction between flat-rate depreciation and reducing-balance depreciation.
Interpret depreciation graphs showing value against time.

callouts.p: A reduction in the value of an asset over time.

analogy.t: The Dimming and Brightening Spotlight Analogy
analogy.p: Imagine a theater spotlight whose brightness can be adjusted. If the light starts at 100 units and increases by 20%, it gains 20 units to reach 120 (multiplier 1.20). To reverse this and get back to 100, you cannot just subtract 20 units from 120; you must take a 16.67% slice of the *new* 120-unit brightness. Multipliers scale your position on a proportional dimmer switch, where forward movement multiplies by values above 1 and backward movement requires division by that exact same multiplier, mirroring how reverse percentages operate.

terms.d: A proportion calculated out of 100, representing a fraction with a denominator of 100.
A decimal factor used to scale a quantity up or down in percentage calculations.
The proportional growth of a value relative to its original size, expressed as a percentage.
The proportional reduction of a value relative to its original size, expressed as a percentage.
The ratio of the absolute change to the original value, multiplied by 100.
The process of calculating the original pre-increase or pre-decrease value from a known final value.
Interest calculated solely on the initial principal amount throughout the investment period.
The initial sum of money lent, invested, or borrowed before interest accrues.
The decrease in the monetary value of an asset over time.
A part, share, or number considered in comparative relation to a whole.
Fractions that represent the same proportion or value despite having different numerators and denominators.
The decimal notation of a fraction or percentage value.

mistakes.w: Adding the percentage change directly to find the original value in reverse percentage questions (e.g., subtracting 20% of the final value).
mistakes.r: Divide the final value by the decimal multiplier (e.g., divide by 1.20 for a 20% increase).

mistakes.w: Using the new value as the denominator in percentage change calculations.
mistakes.r: Always use the original starting value as the denominator: ((New - Original) / Original) x 100.

mistakes.w: Treating a 10% increase followed by a 10% increase as a 20% increase.
mistakes.r: Multiply successive multipliers: 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21, representing a 21% total increase.

mistakes.w: Using compound interest formulas for simple interest problems.
mistakes.r: Simple interest calculates fixed interest on the principal every year: I = PRT / 100.

mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate steps in calculator papers.
mistakes.r: Keep full calculator memory values until the final answer is rounded to the required degree of accuracy.

mistakes.w: Failing to convert percentage rates to decimals before multiplying in interest formulas.
mistakes.r: Divide the percentage rate by 100 (or use R/100) before multiplying.

exam.q: Work out 35% of 420 without using a calculator.
exam.tip: Break percentages into 10% and 5% blocks clearly.

exam.q: A jacket in a sale is priced at 68 pounds after a 15% discount. Calculate the original price of the jacket before the sale.
exam.tip: Remember this is a reverse percentage; divide by the multiplier, never multiply.

exam.q: The price of a house increases from 180,000 pounds to 207,000 pounds. Calculate the percentage increase.
exam.tip: The denominator must be 180000 (the original value).

exam.q: Aiden invests 4000 pounds in an account paying simple interest at a rate of 3.5% per year. Calculate the total amount in the account after 4 years.
exam.tip: Remember to add the interest back onto the principal to find the total amount.

exam.q: Convert 5/8 to a percentage.
exam.tip: Learn standard eighths: 1/8 = 12.5%, so 5/8 = 5 x 12.5% = 62.5%.

exam.q: Decrease 550 by 12%.
In a school, the number of students increases from 850 to 935. Find the percentage increase.
exam.tip: Always check if your answer is an increase or decrease.

exam.q: An investment earns simple interest of 4% per annum. If the total simple interest after 5 years is 600 pounds, find the original principal invested.
exam.tip: Set up the simple interest formula as an algebraic equation.

exam.q: A car depreciates in value by 20% in year one and then by 15% in year two. Calculate the overall percentage decrease over the two years.
exam.tip: Successive percentage changes multiply their multipliers; do not add percentages.

exam.q: Express 7/20 as a percentage and a decimal.
exam.tip: Scale denominator to 100 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 5.

worked.q: A digital tablet is sold for 276 pounds in a sale after a 8% price reduction. What was the original price before the sale?
steps: Identify that a 8% reduction means the sale price represents 92% of the original price (100% - 8%).
Write down the decimal multiplier for this reduction: 0.92.
Set up the equation: Original Price x 0.92 = 276.
Rearrange and calculate: Original Price = 276 / 0.92 = 300 pounds.

worked.q: Chloe invests 2500 pounds in a simple interest account at a rate of 4.2% per year. Calculate the total balance of the account after 6 years.
steps: State the simple interest formula: I = P x R x T / 100.
Calculate interest: I = (2500 x 4.2 x 6) / 100 = 630 pounds.
Add interest to the principal: Total = 2500 + 630 = 3130 pounds.
